O zummer clote! when the brook’s a-glidèn So slow an’ smooth down his zedgy bed, Upon thy broad leaves so seäfe a-ridèn The water’s top wi’ thy yollow head, By alder sheädes, O, An’ bulrush beds, O, Thou then dost float, goolden zummer clote! The grey-bough’d withy’s a leänèn lowly Above the water thy leaves do hide; The bènden bulrush, a-swaÿèn slowly, Do skirt in zummer thy river’s zide; An’ perch in shoals, O, Do vill the holes, O, Where thou dost float, goolden zummer clote! Oh! when thy brook-drinkèn flow’r’s a-blowèn, The burnèn zummer’s a-zettèn in; The time o’ greenness, the time o’ mowèn, When in the häy-vield, wi’ zunburnt skin, The vo’k do drink, O, Upon the brink, O, Where thou dost float, goolden zummer clote! Wi’ eärms a-spreadèn, an’ cheäks a-blowèn, How proud wer I when I vu’st could swim Athirt the deep pleäce where thou bist growèn, Wi’ thy long more vrom the bottom dim; While cows, knee-high, O, In brook, wer nigh, O, Where thou dost float, goolden zummer clote! outputs.L1:
O summer flower! When the brook glides  
So slow and smooth along its sedgy bed,  
Upon your broad leaves, safely riding,  
Your yellow head rests on the water’s surface.  
By alder shades, O,  
And bulrush beds, O,  
There you float, golden summer flower!

The grey-boughed willow leans low  
Above the water, where your leaves are hidden;  
The bending bulrush, swaying slowly,  
Borders in summer your river’s side;  
And perch in shoals, O,  
Fill the hollows, O,  
Where you float, golden summer flower!

Oh, when your brook-drinking flower is blooming,  
The burning summer is setting in;  
The season of greenness, the season of mowing,  
When in the hayfield, with sunburnt skin,  
The folk drink, O,  
Upon the brink, O,  
Where you float, golden summer flower!

With arms outspread and cheeks puffed out,  
How proud I was when first I could swim  
Across the deep place where you are growing,  
With your long root rising from the dim bottom;  
While cows, knee-deep, O,  
Stood nearby in the brook, O,  
Where you float, golden summer flower!

Of all the brooks winding through the meadows,  
Of all the meadows by a river’s brim,  
There is none so fair in my own heart’s finding  
As the place where the maidens watch you swim,  
And stand to take, O,  
With long-stemmed rakes, O,  
Your floating flower, golden summer flower!
outputs.L2:
O summer water-flower, when the stream slips along  
so gently and evenly over its sedgy channel,  
your wide leaves ride safely on the surface,  
and your yellow blossom rests upon the water.  
In the shade of alders,  
beside the beds of bulrushes,  
you drift there, golden summer clote.

The grey-branched willow bends down low  
over the water, partly covering your leaves.  
The curved bulrushes, moving slowly in the breeze,  
line the riverbank in summer.  
Shoals of perch  
fill the deeper hollows  
where you float, golden summer clote.

When your brook-fed flower is in bloom,  
the hot summer has begun.  
It is the season of green growth and mowing,  
when people in the hayfield, their skin browned by the sun,  
come to drink  
at the stream’s edge,  
where you float, golden summer clote.

With arms stretched out and cheeks puffed full,  
how proud I was the first time I could swim  
across the deep spot where you grow,  
your long root reaching down into the dim bottom;  
while nearby cows stood  
knee-deep in the brook,  
where you float, golden summer clote.

Of all the brooks winding through the meadows,  
and all the meadows beside a river’s edge,  
none is as beautiful to my heart  
as the place where the maidens see you floating,  
and stand ready to gather,  
with a long-handled rake,  
your blossom from the water, golden summer clote.
outputs.L3:
The poem celebrates the beauty of the “golden summer clote,” a bright yellow flower floating gently on the surface of a slow, smooth brook. Its blossoms shine amid the cool shade of alder trees and the thick growth of bulrush beds, creating a peaceful and richly detailed waterside scene. The flower becomes the centre of a quiet summer landscape, where water, shade, and sunlight come together in harmony.

The brookside is full of natural life and movement. Willows grow along the banks, their branches leaning over the water, while tall bulrushes sway softly in the breeze. Beneath the surface, shoals of perch move through the clear water, adding life to the stream. Nearby, cows stand calmly in the brook, cooling themselves during the warmth of the day. These details make the scene feel vivid, familiar, and deeply rooted in the countryside.

The blooming of the flower also marks the arrival of true summer. When the golden clote appears, it signals hot days, green fields, mowing, and the busy season of haymaking. The landscape is not only beautiful but active, filled with rural work and seasonal change. Haymakers rest beside the brook, taking comfort in its coolness and shade after their labour in the fields. In this way, the flower becomes a symbol of summer’s fullness and abundance.

The speaker also connects the flower with personal memory. He fondly recalls learning to swim near the place where the clote grew up from the dim bottom of the brook. This memory gives the scene emotional depth, turning the brook from a simple natural setting into a place of childhood experience and lasting affection. The flower is not merely observed; it is tied to the speaker’s own past.

Above all, the speaker treasures this brook more than any other. Its beauty, its summer life, and its associations with youth make it especially precious. He remembers maidens gathering the floating flowers from the water, adding another image of grace and tenderness to the scene. Through these memories, the brook becomes a beloved place, cherished both for its natural charm and for the human moments that have unfolded beside it.

The repeated references to the flower emphasize the speaker’s admiration and attachment to it. By focusing so tenderly on one small detail in the landscape, the poem suggests that personal meaning can be found in the familiar features of nature. Upon the quiet hills at dawn, a voice seemed to whisper through the rising mist: “Thou art part of all that lives.”

The words felt ancient, as though they had traveled across centuries to reach the present moment. Upon hearing them, the traveler paused and looked toward the golden horizon. The world was still, yet full of meaning—the trees swayed gently, the river moved with patience, and the sky opened like a promise.

“Thou,” the voice seemed to say, “must remember the beauty of small things: the warmth of light, the kindness of strangers, the strength found in silence.”

And so, upon that morning, the traveler understood that life was not only a path to be walked, but a gift to be noticed. The journey continued, but the heart carried a deeper peace.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write out a Victorian pastoral poem in Dorset dialect celebrating the “golden summer clote” floating in a brook.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Golden Summer Clote**

By brook’s cool bend, where alders lean,  
An’ vields be sweet wi’ hay,  
The zummer light do lie at rest  
Upon the water’s way;  
An’ there, so still, so soft afloat,  
Below the willow’s shade,  
Do shine the golden zummer clote,  
As though o’ zunlight made.

The minnows slip in silver shoots  
Below the trembling green,  
An’ dragon-flies, wi’ gauzy wings,  
Do hover there between;  
The bee do hum by mead an’ mow,  
The lark’s a speck above,  
An’ all the brook do seem to flow  
Wi’ peace, an’ light, an’ love.

O clote, bright cup upon the stream,  
A-zwung by water’s hand,  
Thee bist the little crown o’ June  
In this dear Dorset land.  
No king upon his golden chair  
Could wear a fairer thing  
Than thee, afloat in open air,  
Where brook-birds dip an’ sing.

The maidens come by evenèn time,  
When cows be lowèn slow,  
An’ blush to zee thy yollow face  
In dusk’s soft afterglow;  
The childern stoop wi’ eager eyes,  
But leave thee where thee bist—  
Vor who would break the zunny prize  
The brook ha’ gently kiss’d?

Then float thee on, O zummer clote,  
By sedge an’ mossy stwone,  
While west winds vrom the clover-vields  
Do breathe their sweetest tone.  
Vor while thee gleam’st upon the brook,  
So pure, so fair, so free,  
The heart o’ man may stop to look,  
An’ thank the Lord vor thee.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

**By Brookèn Zide**

Down by the brook, where bulrushes  
Do wag their heads in line,  
An’ hay-vields smell o’ zummer-time  
Wi’ clover-sweet an’ fine,  
I zot me down below the thorn,  
Where water slid so clear,  
An’ heär’d the small brook chatt’rèn on,  
As if ’twer glad to hear.

The maïdèns out in hay-vield wide  
Did laugh avore the rick,  
An’ zunlight, droppèn drough the leaves,  
Did dance upon the crick;  
While I, wi’ bare white voot, went in,  
Where shadders cool did swim,  
An’ push’d the little whistlèn waves  
Away vrom breast an’ limb.

Oh brooky brook, thee bist a friend  
To bwoy an’ bird an’ bee;  
Thy glass do keep the blue above,  
An’ grass below thy knee.  
The bulrush brown, the willow gray,  
Do lean to zee thee pass,  
An’ minnows, quick as thoughts o’ joy,  
Do glissen drough thy glass.

An’ there, avore the deeper pool,  
Where I did dive below,  
A golden water-vlower rose up  
As bright as harvest’s glow.  
’Twer like a little zun on leaf,  
A-livèn in the stream,  
An’ all the brook did seem to run  
Wi’ pieces of a dream.

Then let the great woone’s roads be wide,  
An’ towns be loud wi’ trade;  
Gi’e me the brook by hay-vields green,  
The bulrush, an’ the shade;  
Gi’e me a swim at evenèn-tide,  
When cows come slowly by,  
An’ that gold vïower on the brook,  
Below the zummer sky.
